subject: maths
title: Searching and sorting algorithms
summary: How linear and binary search find an item, how bubble sort and selection sort put a list in order, and how to count comparisons to compare their efficiency.
body:
Every time you search your contacts, sort a playlist by title or look up a word online, a computer is running a **searching** or **sorting algorithm**. With millions of items, the choice of algorithm decides whether you wait a millisecond or a minute — so we measure algorithms by how much work they do.

## Learning objective

By the end of this lesson you can carry out linear search, binary search, bubble sort and selection sort by hand, and count the comparisons each one needs to judge how efficient it is.

## Before you start

You need **Algorithms with variables and loops (Year 8)** (following steps and loops) and **Algorithms for solving equations (Year 9)** (the halving method), plus powers of 2.

**Warm-up**

1. Work out 2⁶.
2. A list has positions 1 to 15. Which position is exactly in the middle?

**Answers:** 1. 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = **64**. 2. (1 + 15) ÷ 2 = **position 8**.

## Think of it like this

### Finding a name in a phone book

To find "Nguyen" in a printed phone book, you don't read every name from the first page. You open near the middle, see "Lee", know Nguyen comes later, and throw away the whole first half in one go. Then you split what is left again. That is binary search. Reading from page 1 onwards is linear search — it works, but it is painfully slow.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a person jumps roughly to the right letter. A computer running binary search always looks at the exact middle item, and it can only compare one item at a time.

## Key ideas

### Measuring an algorithm

An algorithm must give the right answer and must finish. To compare two algorithms we count the number of **comparisons** (times two items are compared) in the **worst case** — the most work the algorithm could ever need for a list of n items.

### Linear search

**Linear search** (also called sequential search) checks the items one at a time from the start until it finds the target or runs out of items. It works on any list, sorted or not. In the worst case (the target is last, or not there at all) it needs **n comparisons**.

![Linear search for 18 in the list 12, 7, 30, 18, 25, 3, 21: the first three boxes are checked, and 18 is found on the 4th check](/diagrams/y10/maths/searching-and-sorting-algorithms-linear.svg)

### Binary search

**Binary search** only works on a **sorted** list. Look at the middle item (positions low to high: middle = (low + high) ÷ 2, rounded down).

1. If it is the target, stop — found.
2. If the target is smaller, throw away the middle item and everything to its right.
3. If the target is bigger, throw away the middle item and everything to its left.
4. Repeat with the part that is left. If nothing is left, the target is not in the list.

![Binary search for 47 in a sorted list of 15 numbers: it looks at 35, then 51, then 42, then finds 47 on the 4th look, greying out the discarded half each time](/diagrams/y10/maths/searching-and-sorting-algorithms-binary.svg)

Each look halves the list, so the worst case is the smallest whole number k with **2ᵏ ≥ n + 1**. For 1000 items that is only 10 comparisons, because 2¹⁰ = 1024.

### Bubble sort

**Bubble sort** walks along the list comparing **neighbouring pairs**. If a pair is in the wrong order, it **swaps** them. One walk along the list is called a **pass**. After pass 1 the largest value has "bubbled" to the end; after pass 2 the two largest are in place, and so on. Each pass can stop one place earlier, and the algorithm stops after a pass with no swaps.

![Bubble sort of 5, 2, 8, 1, 4: after pass 1 the list is 2, 5, 1, 4, 8; after pass 2 it is 2, 1, 4, 5, 8; after pass 3 it is 1, 2, 4, 5, 8; pass 4 makes no swaps](/diagrams/y10/maths/searching-and-sorting-algorithms-bubble.svg)

For n items the worst case is (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = **n(n − 1) ÷ 2** comparisons.

### Selection sort

**Selection sort** finds the **smallest** item in the unsorted part and swaps it into the first unsorted position. After pass k, the first k items are in their final places. It always makes n(n − 1) ÷ 2 comparisons, but at most n − 1 swaps.

### Comparing efficiency

| Items n | Linear search (worst) | Binary search (worst) | Bubble or selection sort (comparisons) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 10 | 4 | 45 |
| 100 | 100 | 7 | 4950 |
| 1000 | 1000 | 10 | 499 500 |
| 1 000 000 | 1 000 000 | 20 | about 500 billion |

Doubling n doubles linear search, adds just **1** to binary search, and roughly **quadruples** bubble and selection sort.

## Worked examples

### Example 1

Use linear search to find 18 in the list 12, 7, 30, 18, 25, 3, 21. How many comparisons are needed? What is the worst case for this list?

Step 1: compare 18 with 12, then 7, then 30 — none match, so keep going.
Step 2: the 4th comparison is with 18 — match, so stop.
Step 3: so **4 comparisons**. The worst case is **7** — if the target were last or missing, every item would be checked.

### Example 2

Use binary search to find 47 in the sorted list 4, 9, 13, 17, 22, 26, 31, 35, 38, 42, 47, 51, 56, 60, 64 (positions 1 to 15).

Step 1: middle of 1 to 15 is position 8, which holds 35. 47 is bigger — so keep positions 9 to 15.
Step 2: middle of 9 to 15 is position 12, which holds 51. 47 is smaller — so keep positions 9 to 11.
Step 3: middle of 9 to 11 is position 10, which holds 42. 47 is bigger — so keep position 11 only.
Step 4: position 11 holds 47 — found after **4 comparisons**.

Check: the worst case for 15 items is 4, because 2⁴ = 16 ≥ 15 + 1 ✓

### Example 3

Carry out the first pass of bubble sort on 5, 2, 8, 1, 4. How many swaps happen?

Step 1: compare 5 and 2 — wrong order, swap: 2, 5, 8, 1, 4.
Step 2: compare 5 and 8 — right order, no swap.
Step 3: compare 8 and 1 — swap: 2, 5, 1, 8, 4.
Step 4: compare 8 and 4 — swap: **2, 5, 1, 4, 8**, with **3 swaps**.

Check: the largest value, 8, is now at the end ✓

### Example 4

Sort 6, 3, 9, 1, 7 with selection sort. How many comparisons does it make in total?

![Selection sort of 6, 3, 9, 1, 7: after pass 1 the list is 1, 3, 9, 6, 7; after pass 2 it is unchanged; after pass 3 it is 1, 3, 6, 9, 7; after pass 4 it is 1, 3, 6, 7, 9](/diagrams/y10/maths/searching-and-sorting-algorithms-selection.svg)

Step 1: the smallest of all five is 1 — swap it with 6: 1, 3, 9, 6, 7 (4 comparisons to find it).
Step 2: the smallest of 3, 9, 6, 7 is 3, already first in that part — no swap (3 comparisons).
Step 3: the smallest of 9, 6, 7 is 6 — swap it with 9: 1, 3, 6, 9, 7 (2 comparisons).
Step 4: the smallest of 9, 7 is 7 — swap: 1, 3, 6, 7, 9 (1 comparison).
Step 5: total = 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = **10 comparisons**, which matches 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10 ✓

## Common mistakes

- **Using binary search on an unsorted list.** Throwing away half only works if everything on one side is known to be smaller. Fix: sort first, or use linear search.
- **Rounding the middle position the wrong way.** Different rounding gives a different sequence of looks. Fix: use the rule you are given — here (low + high) ÷ 2, rounded down.
- **Forgetting to discard the middle item.** After checking it, the new part starts one place after (or ends one place before) the middle.
- **Doing a whole bubble pass in one jump.** Students often swap only the first pair, or jump straight to the sorted list. Fix: move along one pair at a time and write the list after each swap.
- **Mixing up the sorts.** Bubble sort swaps neighbours; selection sort moves the smallest item to the front.

## Tips to remember

- **"Halve it, don't crawl it."** Binary search halves; linear search crawls one by one. (A made-up memory trick.)
- **Powers of 2 table:** 2¹⁰ ≈ one thousand, 2²⁰ ≈ one million. So about 10 looks per thousandfold increase in size.
- **Bubbles rise to the top:** in bubble sort, the biggest value floats to the end on every pass.
- **Selection = select the smallest**, then put it at the front.
- **Handshake count:** n(n − 1) ÷ 2 is the same as the number of handshakes when n people all shake hands — every pair compared once.

## Key terms

- **Algorithm** — a precise list of steps that solves a problem and always finishes.
- **Linear search** — checking items one by one from the start.
- **Binary search** — repeatedly checking the middle of a sorted list and discarding half.
- **Bubble sort** — sorting by swapping neighbouring items that are out of order, pass after pass.
- **Selection sort** — sorting by repeatedly moving the smallest remaining item to the front.
- **Pass** — one trip through the list.
- **Comparison** — one check of two items against each other.
- **Worst case** — the most comparisons an algorithm could need for n items.

## Summary

- Linear search works on any list; worst case n comparisons.
- Binary search needs a sorted list; worst case is the smallest k with 2ᵏ ≥ n + 1.
- Bubble sort swaps out-of-order neighbours; each pass moves the largest remaining value to the end.
- Selection sort moves the smallest remaining value to the front each pass.
- Both sorts need about n(n − 1) ÷ 2 comparisons, so doubling the list roughly quadruples the work.

questions.prompt: Linear search is used to find 17 in the list shown in the diagram. How many comparisons are made, including the one that finds 17?
questions.explanation: Linear search checks 9, then 4, then 17 — found on the 3rd comparison. Answering 1 treats it like binary search, which starts in the middle.
steps: Linear search starts at the first item and checks each item in order.
Check 9 (no), 4 (no), then 17 (yes) — that is 3 comparisons.

mistakes.A: Step 1: linear search starts at the first item, not the middle — checking the middle first is binary search.
mistakes.B: Step 2: count the check of 17 itself too — two items come before it, plus the one where it is found.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the search stops as soon as 17 is found — it does not carry on to the end of the list.

questions.diagram_alt: A list of five boxes holding 9, 4, 17, 12, 6, in positions 1 to 5.

questions.prompt: Binary search can only be used on one of these lists. Which one?
questions.explanation: Binary search needs a sorted list, and only 2, 5, 9, 14, 20 is in increasing order. 5, 2, 9, 14, 20 is tempting, but its first two items are out of order.
steps: Binary search throws away half the list after each look, which only works if the list is sorted.
Check each list for increasing order: only 2, 5, 9, 14, 20 increases all the way.

mistakes.B: Step 1: binary search needs the list in order. This list jumps up and down, so discarding half could throw away the target.
mistakes.C: Step 1: this list is not in order at all — binary search would not work on it.
mistakes.D: Step 1: check every neighbouring pair — 5 comes before 2, so this list is not sorted.

questions.prompt: Bubble sort is used to sort the list in the diagram into increasing order. What is the list after the first comparison?
questions.explanation: 7 and 3 are out of order, so they swap, giving 3, 7, 9, 2. The answer 3, 7, 2, 9 is the list after the whole pass, not after one comparison.
steps: Compare the first pair, 7 and 3: 7 is bigger, so they are in the wrong order.
Swap them: the list becomes 3, 7, 9, 2.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 7 is bigger than 3, so they are in the wrong order and must be swapped.
mistakes.B: Step 2: one comparison only swaps one pair — the whole list is not sorted yet.
mistakes.C: Step 2: that is the list after the whole first pass. The question asks about the first comparison only.

questions.diagram_alt: A list of four boxes holding 7, 3, 9, 2, with the first two boxes, 7 and 3, highlighted for comparison.

questions.prompt: Binary search is used to find 46 in the sorted list shown. The middle position is (low + high) ÷ 2, rounded down. Which numbers are compared with 46, in order?
questions.explanation: Positions 1–11 → middle 6 (34); 46 is bigger, so 7–11 → middle 9 (52); smaller, so 7–8 → middle 7 (40); bigger, so position 8 holds 46. Rounding 7.5 up would skip 40.
steps: Middle of 1 to 11 is position 6, which holds 34. 46 is bigger, so keep positions 7 to 11.
Middle of 7 to 11 is position 9, which holds 52. 46 is smaller, so keep positions 7 to 8.
Middle of 7 to 8 is 7.5, rounded down to position 7, which holds 40. 46 is bigger, so keep position 8.
Position 8 holds 46 — found. The numbers compared are 34, 52, 40, 46.

mistakes.A: Step 3: (7 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7.5 must be rounded DOWN to position 7, not up to 8.
mistakes.C: Step 2: after 34, look at the middle of positions 7 to 11 (position 9), not the next item along.
mistakes.D: Step 1: that is linear search. Binary search starts at the middle position.

questions.diagram_alt: A sorted list of 11 boxes: 3, 8, 15, 21, 27, 34, 40, 46, 52, 60, 71, with positions 1 to 11 underneath.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows a list before bubble sort starts. What is the list after the first pass?
questions.explanation: The 6 is swapped past 1, 5, 3 and 2 in turn, ending at the back: 1, 5, 3, 2, 6. The list 1, 3, 2, 5, 6 is what you get after a second pass.
steps: Compare 6 and 1: swap → 1, 6, 5, 3, 2. Compare 6 and 5: swap → 1, 5, 6, 3, 2.
Compare 6 and 3: swap → 1, 5, 3, 6, 2. Compare 6 and 2: swap → 1, 5, 3, 2, 6.

mistakes.A: Step 2: one pass does not fully sort the list — it only guarantees the largest value reaches the end.
mistakes.B: Step 2: keep going after the first swap — compare every neighbouring pair along the list.
mistakes.D: Step 2: that is the list after the second pass. Stop after one walk along the list.

questions.diagram_alt: A list of five boxes holding 6, 1, 5, 3, 2.

questions.prompt: A sorted list has 100 items. What is the greatest number of comparisons binary search could need?
questions.explanation: You need the smallest k with 2ᵏ ≥ 101: 2⁶ = 64 is too small and 2⁷ = 128 is enough, so 7. Answering 6 rounds down instead of up.
steps: Binary search worst case: the smallest whole number k with 2ᵏ ≥ n + 1 = 101.
2⁶ = 64 is too small, but 2⁷ = 128 ≥ 101, so the answer is 7.

mistakes.B: Step 1: binary search halves the list every look — 50 is just half of 100, after only one look.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 100 is the worst case for linear search, not binary search.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 2⁶ = 64 is less than 101, so 6 looks cannot cover 100 items. Round up, not down.

questions.prompt: Selection sort is used on the list in the diagram (sorting into increasing order). What is the list after the second pass?
questions.explanation: Pass 1 swaps 2 with 8: 2, 5, 8, 9, 4. Pass 2 finds 4 as the smallest of 5, 8, 9, 4 and swaps it with 5: 2, 4, 8, 9, 5. The answer 2, 5, 4, 8, 9 comes from using bubble sort instead.
steps: Pass 1: the smallest of all is 2 — swap it with the first item, 8: 2, 5, 8, 9, 4.
Pass 2: the smallest of 5, 8, 9, 4 is 4 — swap it with 5: 2, 4, 8, 9, 5.

mistakes.A: Step 2: two passes only fix the first two positions — the rest is not sorted yet.
mistakes.B: Step 1: that is after one pass. Do the second pass: find the smallest of 5, 8, 9, 4.
mistakes.C: Step 1: that is bubble sort after two passes. Selection sort moves the smallest item to the front.

questions.diagram_alt: A list of five boxes holding 8, 5, 2, 9, 4.

questions.prompt: In the worst case, how many comparisons does bubble sort make to sort 20 items (each pass stopping one place earlier than the last)?
questions.explanation: The passes make 19 + 18 + … + 1 = 20 × 19 ÷ 2 = 190 comparisons. 380 forgets to halve.
steps: The passes make 19, 18, 17, …, 1 comparisons.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 20 × 20 compares each item with itself and every pair twice. Use n(n − 1) ÷ 2.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 20 × 19 counts each pair twice — divide by 2.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 19 is the comparisons in the first pass only. Add up all the passes: 19 + 18 + … + 1.

questions.prompt: A sorted list holds 500 names, and a name that is NOT in the list is searched for. How many more comparisons does linear search need than binary search, in the worst case?
questions.explanation: Linear search checks all 500. Binary search needs the smallest k with 2ᵏ ≥ 501, which is 9 (2⁹ = 512). 500 − 9 = 491. Using 8 forgets that 2⁸ = 256 is too small.
steps: Linear search: a missing name means all 500 names are checked.
Binary search: 2⁸ = 256 is too small, 2⁹ = 512 ≥ 501, so 9 comparisons.
Difference: 500 − 9 = 491.

mistakes.B: Step 1: the worst case for linear search is all 500 items, not half of them.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 2⁸ = 256 is less than 501, so binary search needs 9 looks, not 8.
mistakes.D: Step 2: binary search halves the list every look — it needs far fewer than 250 comparisons.

questions.prompt: Binary search on a sorted list of 4000 items needs at most 12 comparisons. The list grows to 8000 items. What is the greatest number of comparisons now?
questions.explanation: One extra look halves 8000 back to 4000, so the answer is 12 + 1 = 13 (check: 2¹³ = 8192 ≥ 8001). Doubling to 24 confuses binary search with linear search.
steps: Check the old list: 2¹² = 4096 ≥ 4001, so 12 looks.
For 8000 items: 2¹² = 4096 is too small, but 2¹³ = 8192 ≥ 8001, so 13 looks — one more than before.

mistakes.A: Step 2: doubling the list only adds one halving step — it does not double the number of looks.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 2¹² = 4096 is less than 8001, so 12 looks are no longer enough.
mistakes.D: Step 2: that is how a sort grows (about four times the work). Binary search grows by one look when the list doubles.

questions.prompt: A computer takes 2 seconds to bubble sort 1000 items in the worst case. Roughly how long would it take to bubble sort 3000 items in the worst case?
questions.explanation: Comparisons = n(n − 1) ÷ 2, roughly n² ÷ 2, so 3 times the items means about 3² = 9 times the work: 2 × 9 = 18 seconds. 6 seconds assumes the work grows in proportion to n.
steps: Worst-case comparisons = n(n − 1) ÷ 2: 499 500 for 1000 items and 4 498 500 for 3000 items.
That is about 9 times as many (4 498 500 ÷ 499 500 ≈ 9.0), so the time is about 2 × 9 = 18 seconds.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the work is not proportional to n. The comparisons grow like n², so 3 times the items is about 9 times the work.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 3 times the items gives about 3² = 9 times the work, not 2³ = 8.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the comparisons grow like n², not n³ — multiply by 9, not 27.

questions.prompt: Bubble sort is run on a list of 8 numbers, and the first pass makes no swaps at all. What can you conclude?

options.A: Only the largest value is in its final place
options.B: Bubble sort still needs n − 1 more passes
options.C: The list must be in reverse order
options.D: The list was already sorted, so bubble sort can stop

questions.explanation: No swaps means every neighbouring pair is in order, so the whole list is in increasing order and the algorithm can stop. "Only the largest value is in place" is true after any pass, but here everything is in place.
steps: A swap happens only when a neighbouring pair is out of order.
No swaps on the first pass means every neighbouring pair is in order, so the list is already sorted and bubble sort can stop.

mistakes.A: Step 2: with no swaps, every neighbouring pair is already in order — so every value is in place, not just the largest.
mistakes.B: Step 2: n − 1 passes is only the worst case. A pass with no swaps means the list is sorted, so stop.
mistakes.C: Step 1: a list in reverse order gives the MOST swaps, because every neighbouring pair is out of order.
